source.title: Minimum Cost to Split into Ones

teaching.hint: Can the cost of a split be interpreted as counting something that happens once over the whole process?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: A split of groups of sizes a and b separates exactly a×b pairs of original unit items, and every pair is separated exactly once.
solution_outline.approach: View the initial number as n labeled unit items. Count the pairs separated by all splits; return the number of unordered pairs of items.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: At any point, each original pair is either still in one piece or has already been separated, and separated pairs never reunite.
solution_outline.correctness: The split charge counts exactly the newly separated cross-piece pairs. Every pair starts together and ends in different singleton pieces, so each contributes exactly one to total cost regardless of split order.
solution_outline.complexity: O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space; the maximum answer for n=500 is 124,750.
solution_outline.pitfall: Choosing the most balanced or most unbalanced split cannot change the total cost.

common_wrong_turns: Treat n=1 as requiring a split
source_fidelity_notes: The positive-part split rule, final all-ones condition, and n=1 boundary are explicit.
